rules.noInventedAgronomy: No symptom, colour, lesion size, temperature or threshold in this file was invented, estimated, averaged or remembered. Every agronomic statement was read from a page that was actually fetched during this pass, and the fetched text is reproduced in `publishedSymptoms` so the tag mapping is auditable without re-fetching. Where a fact could not be sourced the array is EMPTY and the failure is written into `gaps`.
rules.verbatimCapture: TNAU pages were fetched as raw HTML with curl and de-tagged locally, not read through a summarising model, because a summariser silently rewords symptom text — exactly the class of error that would put an unsourced phrase into the KB. The TNAU horticulture PDF was parsed with pypdf. Two pages (Crop Protection Network, UF/IFAS) were read through WebFetch and their `note` says so.
rules.noProse: This file stores i18n KEYS only. The English strings live in i18n.diseases.part-ccm.json. The API never returns display prose (CropRegistry.js: 'i18n key arrays — the API never returns display prose').
rules.noDosage: docs/ai/ai-safety.md rule 3: 'No dosage generation anywhere (pesticide or fertilizer).' No `nextSteps` key contains a dose, a concentration, a product name or a pesticide brand. Where a source recommends chemical control, the published recommendation is NOT reproduced; the farmer is routed to KVK / Kisan Call Centre 1800-180-1551. The fetched chemical recommendations were read and are deliberately discarded.
rules.noUnitConversion: Published measurements are recorded in the unit the source printed. TNAU prints northern-leaf-blight lesions as '1 to 6 inches' and Crop Protection Network prints grey-leaf-spot lesions as 'up to 2 inches'; both are kept in inches. Converting to centimetres would put a computed number into the file (backend/src/knowledge/README.md: nothing is 'estimated, averaged, converted, rounded or inferred').
rules.closedTagVocabulary: symptomTags come from the CLOSED list in the research brief, consumed by the rule-based symptom engine (docs/ai/fallback-strategy.md, weights: pattern 3, part 2, colour 2, distribution 1, weather 1). No tag was invented. Where a published concept has no tag, the concept is left untagged and the miss is recorded in `gaps` (G-TAG-1..G-TAG-4).
rules.tagDerivation: Every entry carries a `tagDerivation` line naming the phrase in `publishedSymptoms` that justifies each tag. A tag with no phrase behind it is a fabrication and none is present.
rules.hindi: Every `names.hi` is null and every entry is `hiVerified: false`. No Hindi-language official source was fetched in this pass, and CLAUDE.md rule 8 forbids unsourced agronomic translation. See gap G-HI-1.
rules.confidenceCodes: P = primary/official Indian government, ICAR or State Agricultural University source. S = everything else, including TNAU-authored courseware hosted off the .ac.in domain (eagri.org) and non-Indian extension bodies. Grading is deliberately conservative: an under-claimed P is harmless, an over-claimed one is not.

datasetCaveats.statement: The two chilli image sources are separable at 0.91 accuracy from a single background statistic alone. CHILLI_ANTHRACNOSE exists ONLY in chilli_secondary; CHILLI_BACTERIAL_SPOT, CHILLI_NUTRIENT_DEFICIENCY and CHILLI_POWDERY_MILDEW exist ONLY in chilli_primary. datasetCaveats.residualRisk: Quoted verbatim from the manifest: 'Not removed, only contained. The only complete fix is chilli imagery of the same classes from a second capture style — no such data exists in the corpus.' The mitigations applied (source-stratified splits, per-class source composition recorded, chilli held at GENERAL tier) CONTAIN the confound; they do not solve it.
datasetCaveats.obligationOnThisKb: A KB entry does not repair a data confound. Metrics for those four chilli classes must be reported with this confound stated and must not be presented as evidence of disease-discrimination ability; the Grad-CAM background-reliance probe (docs/ml/error-analysis.md) is REQUIRED before any chilli accuracy figure is published. CHILLI is GENERAL tier — no field-robustness claim.

datasetCaveats.statement: COTTON is SPECIALIZED tier with 6 classes and 'Ships only once each has a KB entry (en+hi) and the agronomist items (a)-(c) are signed off.' This file supplies the 6 English KB entries. It does NOT supply the Hindi half (every names.hi is null, see G-HI-1) and it does NOT constitute the agronomist sign-off.
outstandingSignOff: (a) three classes never visually reviewed — COTTON_CURL_VIRUS, COTTON_HERBICIDE_DAMAGE, COTTON_LEAF_REDDENING
(b) 39 near-identical image pairs labelled COTTON_CURL_VIRUS in one and COTTON_HEALTHY in the other — early curl virus on a still-green leaf
(c) whether COTTON_LEAF_REDDENING (physiological/nutritional) and COTTON_HERBICIDE_DAMAGE should ship as diagnoses carrying treatment advice at all, versus being reported as observations

names.en: Fruit Rot and Die Back (chilli anthracnose)

diseases.publishedName: TNAU publishes this as 'Fruit Rot and Die Back: Colletotrichum capsici'. The word 'anthracnose' does not appear on either TNAU page fetched; the dataset class code is CHILLI_ANTHRACNOSE and the two are treated as the same problem on the strength of the shared causal organism Colletotrichum capsici.
diseases.publishedSymptoms: TNAU Agritech (chilli_diseases_2.html), verbatim: 'As the fungus causes necrosis of tender twigs from the tip backwards the disease is called die-back Infection usually begins when the crop is in flower. Flowers drop and dry up. There is profuse shedding of flowers. The flower stalk shrivel and dry up. This drying up spreads from the flower stalks to the stem and subsequently causes die-back of the branches and stem and the branches wither. Partia1lly affected plants bear fruits which are few and of low quality. On the surface of the soil the necrotic areas are found separated from the healthy area by a dark brown to black band.' — TNAU horticulture PDF p. 317, verbatim: 'Necrosis of tender twigs from the tip backwards, profuse shedding of flowers. Drying up spreads from the flower stalks to the stem and subsequently causes die-back of the branches and stem which later on wither. Partially affected plants bear few fruits of low quality. Fruits rot appears on ripe fruits where small circular spost initially appear and spreads as oblong black greenish colour or markedly delimited by a black or straw colored area. Badly diseased fruits turn straw coloured with less pungency. The diseased fruist later shrivels nad dries up.' Favourable conditions (same PDF): 'Seed borne and secondary spread by wind during [periods sof high humidity accompanied with rain. Disease appears after rains has stopped nad when there is prolonged deposition of dew on plant.'
diseases.tagDerivation: part:FRUIT ← 'Fruits rot appears on ripe fruits'; part:STEM ← 'die-back of the branches and stem'; part:FLOWER ← 'profuse shedding of flowers'; pattern:SPOTS ← 'small circular spost initially appear'; pattern:ROT ← 'Fruit Rot' / 'Fruits rot appears on ripe fruits'; color:BLACK ← 'oblong black greenish colour or markedly delimited by a black or straw colored area'; color:TAN ← 'straw coloured' (the closed vocabulary has no STRAW member; TAN is its nearest member and the mapping is asserted here, not by the source); weather:HIGH_HUMIDITY ← 'periods sof high humidity'; weather:RAIN ← 'accompanied with rain'. NO part:LEAF tag: neither TNAU page describes any leaf lesion for this disease (see G-CA-1).

names.en: Bacterial blight (angular leaf spot / black arm)

diseases.publishedName: TNAU: 'Bacterial blight: Xanthomonas campestris p.v malvacearum'. The eagri courseware names the same disease 'Xanthomonas axonopodis pv. malvacearum'; the two names are the same organism under different nomenclature and neither is preferred here.
diseases.publishedSymptoms: TNAU Agritech (cotton_d9.html), verbatim, five published phases: 'The bacterium attacks all stages from seed to harvest.' 1. Seedling blight — 'Small, water-soaked, circular or irregular lesions on the cotyledons. Infection spreads to stem through petiole and cause withering and death of seedlings.' 2. Angular Leaf Spot — 'Small, dark green, water soaked areas develop on lower surface of leaves. The spots become angular restricted by veins and veinlets and are visible on both the surface of leaves. Later they turn reddish brown colour and infection spreads to veins and veinlets.' 3. Vein necrosis or Vein banding — 'Blackening of the veins and veinlets, gives a typical ‘blighting’ appearance. On the lower surface of the leaf, bacterial oozes are formed as crusts or scales. The leaves become crinkled and twisted inward and show withering. The infection also spreads from veins to petiole and cause blighting leading to defoliation.' 4. Blackarm — 'On the stem and fruiting branches, dark brown to black lesions are formed. Girdle the stem and branches to cause premature drooping off of the leaves. Cracking of stem and gummosis, resulting in breaking of the stem and hang typically as dry black twig to give a characteristic “black arm” symptom.' 5. Square rot or boll rot — 'On the bolls, water soaked lesions appear and turn into dark black and sunken irregular spots. Infection slowly spreads to entire boll and shedding occurs. Infection on mature bolls lead to premature bursting. The bacterium spreads inside the boll and lint gets stained yellow because of bacterial ooze and loses its appearance and market value.' Favourable conditions, verbatim: 'Optimum soil temperature of 28˚C, High atmospheric temperature of 30-40˚C, Relative humidity of 85 per cent, Poor tillage, late irrigation, Potassium deficiency in soil. Rain followed by bright sunshine during the months of October and November.'
diseases.tagDerivation: part:LEAF ← 'water soaked areas develop on lower surface of leaves'; part:STEM ← 'On the stem and fruiting branches, dark brown to black lesions are formed'; part:FRUIT ← 'On the bolls, water soaked lesions appear' (the boll is the fruit); pattern:SPOTS ← 'The spots become angular'; pattern:LESIONS ← 'dark brown to black lesions are formed'; pattern:ROT ← 'Square rot or boll rot'; pattern:CURL ← 'The leaves become crinkled and twisted inward'; color:BROWN ← 'turn reddish brown colour'; color:BLACK ← 'Blackening of the veins and veinlets' and 'dry black twig'; color:RED ← 'reddish brown'; color:YELLOW ← 'lint gets stained yellow'; distribution:VEINS ← 'restricted by veins and veinlets' and 'Blackening of the veins and veinlets'; weather:HIGH_HUMIDITY ← 'Relative humidity of 85 per cent'; weather:RAIN ← 'Rain followed by bright sunshine during the months of October and November'. NO weather:HOT_DRY despite 'High atmospheric temperature of 30-40˚C', because that tag also asserts dryness and the same source requires 85% RH.
diseases.differentialCaveat: pattern:CURL is genuinely published for this disease ('crinkled and twisted inward') and is tagged, so a farmer reporting leaf curl on cotton will legitimately see bacterial blight alongside COTTON_CURL_VIRUS and COTTON_LEAF_HOPPER_JASSIDS. The discriminating published features are the angular vein-bounded water-soaked spots and the black veins, neither of which the other two carry.

names.en: Leaf reddening (red leaf) — a disorder, not a disease

diseases.publishedName: ICAR publishes this as 'Red leaf symptoms in cotton', abbreviated RLS in the abstract. ADR-021 describes the dataset class as 'Leaf Redding (physiological/nutritional)'.
diseases.publishedSymptoms: ICAR, Indian Farming 60(9) 2010, Praharaj & Sankaranarayanan, abstract verbatim: 'The cause for the RLS disorder has been both biotic and abiotic factors. The reddening in leaves is attributed to magnesium deficiency, lower leaf N content, sudden fall in night temperature, low soil N supply, high temperature during the day coupled with low temperature at night, water stress and waterlogging. However, the biochemical studies proved that reddening of cotton leaves was related to an increased formation of anthocyanin pigments mainly cyanidin glycosides. Foliar application of urea @2%, DAP @2 % and MgSO4@1% at boll development period is helpful for managing leaf reddening symptoms in cotton. Further research is needed to provide a better understanding of factors that influence cotton diseases and to develop management strategies that reduce economic losses.' — NOTE what this does and does not contain: it names CAUSES and biochemistry. It publishes NO description of how the reddening looks or progresses (which leaves, what shade, over how long). Corroborating mechanism from TNAU's nutrition page, verbatim: 'sugars in corn combine with flavones to form anthocyanins (purple, red, and yellow pigments) and their accumulation may be caused by an insufficient supply of P, low soil temperature, insect damage to the roots, or N deficiency.'
diseases.tagDerivation: part:LEAF ← 'reddening of cotton leaves'; color:RED ← 'The reddening in leaves'. That is ALL that is published. No pattern tag is applied because the vocabulary has no member for whole-leaf discolouration and no published phrase supports SPOTS, BLOTCHES, STREAKS or YELLOWING. CONSEQUENCE FOR THE ENGINE: pattern carries weight 3, the largest single term in docs/ai/fallback-strategy.md, so this entry can never score highly and will rarely surface in the rule-based checker. That is an honest reflection of thin sourcing, not a bug to be patched with an invented tag. See G-CLR-1 and G-TAG-4.
diseases.differentialCaveat: Reddening of cotton leaves is also a published symptom of leafhopper attack (TNAU: 'Downward curling and reddening of leaves... turn brick red colour'), and the ICAR abstract itself says the cause is 'both biotic and abiotic factors'. This entry must never be presented as identifying a specific cause.

Note this is also the single chilli class that exists ONLY in chilli_secondary (see DC-CHILLI-CONFOUND).

gaps.field: CHILLI_BACTERIAL_SPOT — no favourable conditions, no distribution
gaps.problem: Neither TNAU source publishes favourable weather conditions or a canopy position for chilli bacterial leaf spot.
gaps.checked: chilli_diseases_4.html (has no 'Favourable Conditions' heading at all); agritech.tnau.ac.in/pdf/9.pdf p. 318.
gaps.impact: The entry carries no weather or distribution tag, so it loses 2 of the engine's possible points and will under-score relative to entries that have them.
gaps.resolution: Left untagged. Not patched from general bacterial-disease knowledge.

gaps.field: CHILLI_NUTRIENT_DEFICIENCY — the source is not about chilli
gaps.problem: The only nutrient-deficiency source located is TNAU's GENERAL mineral-nutrition page. It never mentions chilli. Every symptom in that entry is therefore a general-plant statement attached to a chilli-specific class code.
gaps.checked: Searched for a chilli-specific nutrient-deficiency page on agritech.tnau.ac.in (three candidate URLs, all HTTP 404) and for an ICAR-IIHR chilli nutrition page. The commercial agri portals that do publish chilli-specific deficiency symptoms (Agriplex, Aries Agro, worldofchillies) were deliberately not used — they are vendors.
gaps.impact: The KB text is honest but generic. It cannot say anything chilli-specific about which nutrient is likely in Indian chilli soils.
gaps.resolution: Used with the scope disclosed in the sourceRef, in the datasetCaveats and in the farmer-facing text itself. An ICAR-IIHR or SAU chilli nutrition source would replace it.

gaps.field: CHILLI_NUTRIENT_DEFICIENCY — distribution tag forced to a single choice
gaps.problem: The published symptoms split by nutrient: N, P, K and Mg deficiency show on OLDER (lower) leaves, while Fe and Zn deficiency show on YOUNG (upper) leaves. One class code covers both.
gaps.checked: The full 'Generalized Visual Leaf and Plant Nutrient Element Deficiency and Excess Symptoms' table.
gaps.impact: Only distribution:LOWER_LEAVES is tagged, so a farmer reporting an upper-leaf problem will not match this entry even though the source supports it for Fe/Zn.
gaps.resolution: Tagged LOWER_LEAVES only, because tagging both members of a two-member distinction makes the term carry no information. The alternative — tagging both — is defensible and is left to the engine owner.

gaps.field: CHILLI_POWDERY_MILDEW — prevention array is EMPTY
gaps.problem: Both TNAU sources publish only chemical management for chilli powdery mildew (wettable sulphur, carbendazim, Dinocap). Neither publishes any cultural or preventive practice.
gaps.checked: chilli_diseases_3.html in full (management is two chemical lines); agritech.tnau.ac.in/pdf/9.pdf p. 318 (management is one chemical line).
gaps.impact: This entry ships with no prevention advice. Feature DoD expects loading/empty states to be handled; the UI must render an empty prevention list without implying there is nothing a farmer can do.
gaps.resolution: Left EMPTY rather than filled with generic 'improve air circulation'-style advice, which no fetched source publishes for this crop.

gaps.field: COTTON_CURL_VIRUS — no primary Indian source
gaps.problem: Cotton leaf curl disease is a north-west India problem (Punjab, Haryana, Rajasthan) and TNAU, a Tamil Nadu institution, does not list it among cotton diseases at all. The only fetched page describing its symptoms is TNAU courseware on eagri.org, graded S.
gaps.checked: agritech.tnau.ac.in cotton disease index — 10 diseases, no leaf curl. cicr.org.in — reachable, but /cotton-health-management/ renders as an image slider with no text content, and no CLCuD symptom page was found in its link map. iimr-style deep search on cicr.org.in returned only research papers behind publishers.
gaps.impact: A SPECIALIZED-tier crop's flagship virus class rests on a single secondary citation.
gaps.resolution: Recorded as S with the reasoning in the sourceRef. An ICAR-CICR or PAU package-of-practices page should replace it before cotton ships.

gaps.field: COTTON_HERBICIDE_DAMAGE — no Indian source at all; prevention EMPTY
gaps.problem: No ICAR, ICAR-CICR, SAU or NIPHM document describing herbicide injury symptoms in cotton could be located. The entry rests entirely on a University of Florida extension publication.
gaps.checked: Two web searches targeting CICR/ICAR advisories on 2,4-D and glyphosate drift in cotton; cicr.org.in link map. All returned US extension material or paywalled Weed Technology papers.
gaps.impact: A SPECIALIZED-tier class documented only from US practice, where the herbicide mix, the crop's transgenic tolerance traits and the drift context all differ from India. `prevention` is empty because the only preventive advice available would be spray-practice advice, which this file does not give.
gaps.resolution: Kept as an OBSERVATION with a raised expert threshold and no treatment guidance, pending ADR-021 decision 1(c). This is the entry most in need of Indian sourcing.

gaps.field: COTTON_LEAF_REDDENING — the source publishes causes, not appearance; full text unreachable
gaps.problem: The ICAR abstract names causes and the anthocyanin mechanism but never describes how the reddening looks — which leaves redden first, what shade, how fast it spreads. The full-text PDF at epubs.icar.org.in/index.php/IndFarm/article/download/49106/21048/119672 returned an HTTP 404 body when fetched with curl, so only the abstract could be read.
gaps.checked: Article landing page fetched via WebFetch; PDF download URL fetched via curl (1,339 bytes of HTML beginning '<h1>4...'). No alternate host for Indian Farming 60(9) was found.
gaps.impact: Only one symptom key and only two tags could be written. Because no `pattern` tag is possible, the entry can never score highly in the rule-based engine (pattern carries weight 3).
gaps.resolution: Written thin rather than padded. Retrieving the full text, or an ICAR-CICR red-leaf advisory, would let a proper symptom description and at least one pattern tag be added.

gaps.field: MAIZE_GRAY_LEAF_SPOT — no Indian source; entire entry is secondary
gaps.problem: Grey leaf spot appears on neither Indian maize disease page fetched. This is the only one of the 17 codes with no P citation anywhere in the entry.
gaps.checked: TNAU Agritech maize disease index (Downy mildew/Crazy top, Turcicum Leaf Blight, Charcoal Rot, Common Rust, Aspergillus Rot — no GLS). eagri PATH 272 Lecture 05 maize (11 diseases listed — no GLS). iimr.icar.gov.in did not resolve in DNS (getaddrinfo ENOTFOUND) from this environment, on both curl and WebFetch, so the ICAR-IIMR 'IDM for important diseases of maize' and 'Predominant diseases of maize across India' pages could not be read; www.iimr.res.in resolves but its Crop Protection division page carries no disease descriptions. Two targeted searches for a Karnataka/UAS package-of-practices GLS page returned only US and South African material.
gaps.impact: An Indian farmer would be shown lesion sizes in inches and a tasselling timing derived from US corn agronomy.
gaps.resolution: Shipped as S with the failure stated. RETRY ICAR-IIMR when DNS permits — its pages are the obvious fix and were unreachable for network reasons, not because they lack the content.

gaps.field: MAIZE_NORTHERN_LEAF_BLIGHT — the source page conflates two pathogens
gaps.problem: TNAU's page is headed 'Leaf Blight : Exserohilum turcicum & Helminthosporium maydis'. Those are two different diseases — turcicum (northern) leaf blight and maydis (southern) leaf blight — described under one symptom list. The eagri courseware is worse: it heads its page 'Leaf blight - Helminthosporium maydis (Syn : H. turcicum)', treating the two as synonyms, which they are not, and describes a different symptom picture ('Small yellowish round to oval spots... straw to grayish brown in the centre with dark brown margins').
gaps.checked: agritech.tnau.ac.in/crop_protection/maize_disease_new/maize_2.html and its index heading 'Turcicum Leaf Blight (TLB)'; eagri PATH 272 lecture05/005.html.
gaps.impact: The symptom text used here — cigar-shaped grey-green to tan lesions tapering at the ends — is the classic turcicum description and matches the class, so the entry is very probably right. But it cannot be attributed to Exserohilum turcicum ALONE on the strength of this page, and the eagri page was therefore NOT used for symptoms.
gaps.resolution: TNAU used, index heading recorded as the evidence that TNAU means turcicum, conflation disclosed. An ICAR-IIMR page separating the two would settle it (blocked by the same DNS failure as G-MGLS-1).

gaps.field: CHILLI_HEALTHY / COTTON_HEALTHY / MAIZE_HEALTHY — nothing published describes 'healthy'
gaps.problem: Extension literature describes disease, not health. No page fetched publishes a positive description of what a healthy chilli, cotton or maize leaf looks like.
gaps.checked: All 12 crop-protection pages fetched, plus the TNAU horticulture PDF and TNAU's mineral-nutrition page.
gaps.impact: The 'what healthy looks like' guidance the brief asks for cannot be sourced as an agronomic claim.
gaps.resolution: The healthy entries carry NO symptom text. Their `inspect` keys are scouting actions INVERTED from sourced disease facts — 'turn the leaf over, because powdery mildew and blight both start there', 'start with the lower leaves, because blight and grey leaf spot both start there' — and each inversion names its source in the sourceRefs note. Their `prevention` keys are the published cultural measures from the corresponding disease pages. No claim of the form 'a healthy leaf is uniformly green' is made anywhere, because nothing fetched says it.

gaps.field: symptomTags vocabulary — no INTERVEINAL member
gaps.problem: Both CHILLI_LEAF_CURL_VIRUS ('yellowing between the veins') and CHILLI_NUTRIENT_DEFICIENCY ('interveinal chlorosis (yellowing between the veins)') publish interveinal yellowing. distribution:VEINS reads as 'on/along the veins', which is the opposite placement.
gaps.checked: The closed distribution list: LOWER_LEAVES, UPPER_LEAVES, ALL_LEAVES, SCATTERED, MARGINS, VEINS.
gaps.impact: Interveinal chlorosis — one of the most recognisable and most farmer-answerable symptom patterns there is — cannot be expressed at all.
gaps.resolution: Not tagged. A `distribution:INTERVEINAL` member would fix it; adding one is a vocabulary change and therefore an engine decision, not a data decision.

gaps.field: symptomTags vocabulary — no LEAF_UNDERSIDE member
gaps.problem: CHILLI_POWDERY_MILDEW ('white powdery growth on lower side of leaves'), COTTON_BACTERIAL_BLIGHT ('lower surface of leaves'), COTTON_CURL_VIRUS ('enation on underside of leaves'), MAIZE_NORTHERN_LEAF_BLIGHT ('Spores are produced on the underside of leaf') and MAIZE_COMMON_RUST ('on both leaf surfaces') all publish a LEAF SURFACE. The vocabulary has only canopy positions.
gaps.checked: Same closed distribution list.
gaps.impact: Five of 17 entries lose their most practical inspection cue from the tag layer. distribution:LOWER_LEAVES was NOT used as a substitute anywhere, because it would tell the engine 'lower part of the plant' when the source said 'underside of the leaf'.
gaps.resolution: Not tagged. The underside cue survives in the `inspect` keys, which is where a farmer actually needs it.

gaps.field: symptomTags vocabulary — no SHAPE_DEFORMITY / STRAPPING member
gaps.problem: COTTON_HERBICIDE_DAMAGE's most diagnostic published feature is 'Leaf shape can appear out of proportion (uncharacteristically long and narrow, called strapping)'. CHILLI_LEAF_CURL_VIRUS publishes 'leaves greatly reduced in size'. Neither is expressible; the pattern list covers marks on a leaf, not the leaf's shape or size.
gaps.checked: The closed pattern list, all 14 members.
gaps.impact: Herbicide damage is under-tagged and will be hard to separate from the other curl entries.
gaps.resolution: Not tagged. Recorded for the engine owner.

gaps.field: symptomTags vocabulary — no DISCOLOURATION / REDDENING pattern member
gaps.problem: COTTON_LEAF_REDDENING's entire published symptom is a colour change of the whole leaf. pattern:YELLOWING is the only colour-change member and it names the wrong colour.
gaps.checked: The closed pattern list.
gaps.impact: The entry carries NO pattern tag. Since pattern carries weight 3 — the heaviest term in docs/ai/fallback-strategy.md — this entry is structurally unable to rank. COTTON_LEAF_HOPPER_JASSIDS, which shares the reddening, does carry pattern:CURL and pattern:STUNTING and will therefore always outrank it, which is arguably the safer failure but is not a designed behaviour.
gaps.resolution: Not tagged. Either a generic `pattern:DISCOLOURATION` member, or renaming YELLOWING to a colour-neutral member with the colour carried by the colour tags, would fix it.

gaps.field: symptomTags — MAIZE_NORTHERN_LEAF_BLIGHT and MAIZE_GRAY_LEAF_SPOT are nearly indistinguishable
gaps.problem: The two entries share 7 tags (part:LEAF, pattern:LESIONS, pattern:STREAKS, color:TAN, color:GREY, distribution:LOWER_LEAVES, weather:HIGH_HUMIDITY). The published discriminators are lesion GEOMETRY — cigar-shaped and tapering versus rectangular and vein-bounded — and the vocabulary cannot express shape.
gaps.checked: Both entries' publishedSymptoms, tag by tag, against the closed vocabulary.
gaps.impact: In the rule-based symptom checker these two maize diseases will score almost identically for any answer set a farmer can give. That is not a modelling accident; it is a limit of the question set. Both diseases are managed similarly in the published cultural advice (stubble/residue destruction), so the consequence of confusing them is small — but the app must not present a near-tie as a discrimination.
gaps.resolution: Recorded rather than engineered around. The `inspect` keys for both entries lead with the geometry question ('do the lesion edges stop dead at the veins?' vs 'is the lesion cigar-shaped and tapering?'), which is where the distinction can actually be made.

gaps.field: expertThreshold raised to 0.6 on three entries — PROPOSAL, not a decision
gaps.problem: CHILLI_NUTRIENT_DEFICIENCY, COTTON_HERBICIDE_DAMAGE and COTTON_LEAF_REDDENING carry expertThreshold 0.6 instead of the schema default 0.4. All three are abiotic/broad classes where the source itself declines to discriminate.
gaps.checked: backend/src/models/CropRegistry.js diseaseSchema (default 0.4); docs/ai/fallback-strategy.md ('expert-referral threshold (score <0.4 ... )'); ADR-021 §1(c).
gaps.impact: Raising the threshold routes more farmers to KVK for these three classes. 0.6 is a chosen number, not a measured one — no source publishes an expert-referral threshold for anything.
gaps.resolution: Applied with the reason recorded on each entry, and flagged here as requiring human approval. If the reviewer prefers the uniform default, revert all three to 0.4; nothing else in the file depends on the value.

gaps.field: severity, spread speed, yield-loss figures — not attempted
gaps.problem: No entry carries a severity grade, a spread-rate claim or a yield-loss percentage. Several sources publish qualitative severity ('causing severe reduction in fruit yield', 'resulting in reduced yield') but none publishes a scale this KB could key to, and CLAUDE.md rule 9 makes severity engine-assessed rather than KB-declared.
gaps.checked: All 12 pages plus the horticulture PDF.
gaps.impact: None for the current schema — diseaseSchema has no severity field.
gaps.resolution: Deliberately omitted. If a severity field is ever added it must be sourced or engine-computed, not inherited from adjectives.

gaps.field: Regional applicability of TNAU guidance
gaps.problem: Nine of the 12 primary pages used are TNAU's — Tamil Nadu. Cotton is grown mainly in Maharashtra, Gujarat, Telangana, Punjab and Haryana; maize in Karnataka, Bihar, MP and Telangana. Favourable-condition statements tied to Tamil Nadu's calendar travel worst: the cotton bacterial blight page says 'Rain followed by bright sunshine during the months of October and November', which is a Tamil Nadu north-east-monsoon statement.
gaps.checked: Source institution of every citation.
gaps.impact: Month-specific and season-specific guidance may be wrong outside south India. It is reproduced because it is what the source says, but it is not universal.
gaps.resolution: The month-bound cotton statement is kept inside an `inspect` key (a prompt to look), never inside a `nextSteps` key (an instruction to act). A reviewer covering the cotton belt should re-check it against ICAR-CICR.

verificationChecklistBeforeUse: 1. Fill every names.hi and the entire `hi` object of the i18n file with human-verified Hindi (G-HI-1). COTTON CANNOT SHIP UNTIL THIS IS DONE — manifest support_tiers.COTTON and ADR-021 §1 both require en+hi.
2. Obtain agronomist sign-off on ADR-021 §1 items (a)-(c). Until (c) is signed, COTTON_LEAF_REDDENING and COTTON_HERBICIDE_DAMAGE must stay observations, as written here.
3. Re-source MAIZE_GRAY_LEAF_SPOT from ICAR-IIMR when iimr.icar.gov.in resolves (G-MGLS-1). It is the only entry in this file with no primary citation.
4. Re-source COTTON_HERBICIDE_DAMAGE and COTTON_CURL_VIRUS from Indian institutions (G-CHD-1, G-CCV-1).
5. Decide the four vocabulary gaps G-TAG-1..G-TAG-4 with the engine owner before the rule-based checker is tuned; G-TAG-5 needs a question-set answer, not a data answer.
6. Approve or revert the three raised expertThresholds (G-THRESH-1).
7. Resolve CHILLI_ANTHRACNOSE's missing leaf description (G-CA-1) — it is the class most likely to be predicted from a leaf photo and least able to explain itself.
